content.title: About
content.content: Sweetened almond milk is made from ground almonds, water and added sugar (or another sweetener). It has a mild nutty flavor, light sweetness and a creamy texture, suitable for vegans and people who are lactose intolerant.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almond milk became popular as an alternative beverage in the 1990s when the U.S. vegan movement gained momentum.
Sweetened versions often use cane sugar, maple syrup or fruit juice to add sweetness.
Almonds belong to the Rosaceae family and are more closely related to peaches than to true nuts.
Almond milk contains fewer calories than cow's milk, but sweetened versions have higher sugar content.
Unlike cow's milk, almond milk naturally contains no cholesterol.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Most of the fat in almond milk is monounsaturated, which is heart‑friendly.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Sweetened varieties are often fortified with calcium to support bone health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Almond milk contains a small amount of dietary fiber that can aid regular digestion.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Completely free of lactose, making it suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: People allergic to almonds or other tree nuts may experience severe reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions can contain significant amounts of sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics or those watching their weight.

items.title: Low protein
items.content: Compared with cow's milk, almond milk provides little protein, so it shouldn't be relied on as a primary protein source.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: Some brands use artificial flavors and stabilizers that may cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sweetened almond milk is great as a refreshing drink, added to coffee, tea, smoothies, oatmeal, baked goods, or used in sauces and desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator after opening and consume within 5‑7 days. Unopened cartons can be kept in a cool, dry place until the printed expiration date.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit Flavored Cereal is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast made from whole grains, enhanced with natural fruit aromas and a modest amount of sugar. The flakes are light and crunchy with a sweet‑tart fruit taste, making them popular among both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cereal is produced from a blend of wheat, oats and rice that are heat‑treated to preserve nutrients.
Fruit flavor comes from natural fruit extracts rather than artificial flavorings.
The product is often fortified with B‑vitamins, iron and zinc to support energy metabolism.
Packaging is typically made from recyclable plastic to reduce environmental impact.
Fruit Flavored Cereal is a common choice for school breakfasts because it requires no preparation.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The grains provide slowly digestible carbs that deliver sustained energy and keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B6 and folate support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids normal digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Fortified with iron
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The cereal contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even moderate sugar can raise blood glucose levels in individuals prone to diabetes.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: People allergic to wheat, oats or rice may experience reactions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Contains gluten, so it is not suitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some versions may contain artificial colorants that can be a concern for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the Fruit Flavored Cereal with milk or a plant‑based beverage; add fresh berries, banana slices or nuts for extra nutrition. It can also be used as a base for dessert parfaits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal tightly to prevent moisture absorption.

muffin-english-oat-bran-with-raisins.title: English Oat Bran Muffin with Raisins

content.title: About
content.content: The English oat bran muffin with raisins is a baked good made from whole‑grain flour, oat bran, and dried raisins. It offers a light, airy crumb, a subtle sweetness from the raisins, and a nutty flavor from the bran.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat bran is a by‑product of oat milling and is high in dietary fiber.
Raisins provide natural sweetness and a modest amount of iron.
Muffins are a popular quick‑breakfast or snack option.
The fiber in oat bran can help prolong feelings of fullness.
Traditional recipes avoid artificial flavors and rely on whole ingredients.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oat bran supplies both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Raisins add iron, helping to prevent anemia.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The combination of whole grains and dried fruit leads to a steadier blood‑sugar response.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in oats and raisins help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat flour and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins add natural sugars; individuals monitoring blood glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Muffins can be calorie‑rich due to oil and sugar, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of bran may cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the muffin as a snack on its own, split it and spread with cottage cheese, yogurt, or nut butter. It pairs well with tea or coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months).

potato-boiled-from-fresh-peel-eaten-made.title: Boiled Potato, fresh, peel eaten, with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a tuber widely used in cooking. In this version the potatoes are boiled in salted water, the skin is left on, and the finished dish is dressed with vegetable oil. It is a simple, filling and nutritious product popular in many world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century and quickly became a staple food.
The skin contains more fiber and vitamins than the flesh, so it is often left on.
Boiling potatoes with the skin on preserves more minerals, especially potassium and iron.
Vegetable oil added after cooking improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
In Russia boiled potatoes are traditionally served with sour cream or butter and used in salads.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Boiled potatoes provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: The skin supplies dietary fiber that promotes digestive health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Plain boiled potatoes contain almost no fat; a modest amount of oil makes the dish more balanced.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Complex starches give sustained satiety and energy.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Using too much salt during boiling can increase the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Oil allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to the vegetable oil used for dressing.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Acrylamide can form during prolonged heating in oil, but this risk is minimal when potatoes are boiled with the skin on.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot boiled potatoes drizzled with a small amount of vegetable oil (olive, sunflower) and optionally seasoned with salt and fresh herbs. The skin can be eaten whole or sliced. It works as a standalone snack or as a side dish for meat, fish, or vegetable stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep boiled potatoes in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3–4 days. Reheat in the microwave or on the stovetop before serving. Avoid storing near fruits, which can accelerate oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp Creole is a fragrant Creole‑style dish made with large shrimp, tomatoes, onion, sweet bell pepper, garlic and spices, but without rice. It delivers a rich, slightly spicy flavor with hints of paprika and thyme.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Creole cuisine originated in Louisiana, blending French, Spanish, African and Native American culinary traditions.
Tomatoes in Creole sauce often replace the rarer "cherry tomatoes," giving the dish a vivid color.
Shrimp cook quickly in the sauce—usually 3‑5 minutes—to keep them tender.
Traditionally Creole is served over rice, but the no‑rice version often uses cauliflower rice or quinoa for a low‑carb alternative.
The dish is commonly garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or cilantro for added brightness.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality marine protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Without rice the dish remains low‑calorie, making it suitable for energy‑restricted diets.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp are a good source of EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the shrimp and the Creole spices supply B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomatoes and spices (paprika, garlic) contain lycopene and quercetin, helping combat free radicals.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Traditional Creole sauce can be salty; adjust added salt to taste.

items.title: Foodborne toxins
items.content: Improperly stored shrimp may harbor bacteria that cause food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs. Pair it with vegetable sides, cauliflower rice, or quinoa. A squeeze of lime adds a bright acidity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked Creole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 1 month. Thaw in the fridge and reheat over medium heat.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy nut butter is a spread made from roasted soy nuts that have a flavor and texture similar to traditional nut butters. It is rich in plant protein, healthy fats, and vitamins, making it suitable for vegans and those with nut allergies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy nuts are roasted soybeans processed into a nut‑like paste.
Soy nut butter is often used as a substitute for peanut or almond butter in recipes.
The product is gluten‑free and fits a gluten‑free diet.
Soy nuts are high in isoflavones, which may support hormonal balance.
Compared with many nut butters, soy nut butter is usually more affordable.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One tablespoon provides about 4 g of protein, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains healthy mono‑ and polyunsaturated fats
items.content: These fats support heart health when part of a balanced diet.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Isoflavones may aid hormonal balance and bone health.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Soy nut butter contains virtually no sugar, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from mild to severe, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals if consumed in large amounts.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Like other spreads, soy nut butter is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMO)
items.content: Most soybeans are GMO; choose a non‑GMO labeled product if this is a concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soy nut butter can be spread on toast, added to smoothies, sauces, baked goods, or used as a base for vegan desserts. It also mixes well into oatmeal, yogurt, or fruit bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight jar in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if it develops a rancid smell.
